title: Client - Server Database Models

overview.whatIsIt:
Client - server architecture is a way of organizing a database system where
two kinds of computers work together: a
client (which asks for data) and a
server
(which stores and manages the
data and answers the request).
overview.whyNeed:
Before client
- server systems, all processing happened on one
giant central computer (mainframe), and users only had "dumb terminals" (screens
with no processing power). This was expensive and hard to scale. Client
- server
architecture splits the work, so:
- Many users can work at the same time.
- The heavy
work of storing and protecting data stays in one safe place (the server).
- The client can
have a friendly, fast user interface.
overview.whereUsed:
- Bankin g systems (ATM = client, bank database = server)
- College
portals (your browser = client, college server = server)
- Online shopping websites
-
Almost every modern application that uses a database
overview.importantNotes:
Client - server is not one fixed design
- it comes in different "tiers" (2
- tier,
3- tier), which we will study in detail.

client ) do not cook your own food. You tell
the waiter what you want. The waiter passes your order to the kit
chen (the
server ),

-

subsections.title: 4.1 Two - Tier Client
subsections.content:
- Server Architecture
In a two - tier architecture, there are exactly two layers:
1. Client Tier
- contains the user interface AND the application/business logic.
2. Server Tier
- contains the database (data storage and query processing).
The client talks
directly to the database server, usually using a standard protocol such
as ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) or
JDBC (Java Database Connectivity).
Components:
- Client application (contains UI + business rules)
- Network connection
- Database server (stores data, executes SQL, returns results)
Working: The client builds an SQL query, sends it directly to the database server over
the network, the server executes it and sends back the result set, and the client
displays it.
Advantages: - Simple to build and understand
- Fast for small numbers of users (fewer
hops) - Good for LAN
- based systems within one organization
Limitations:
- Every client machine needs the correct drivers/business logic installed
(hard to update)
- Does not scale
well - too many direct connections overload the
server - Business logic mixed with UI code makes maintenance difficult
- Security risk
- clients directly touch the database

subsections.title: 4.2 Three - Tier Client
subsections.content:
- Server Architecture
In a three - tier architecture, the work is split into three separate layers:
1. Presentation Tier (Client)
- only handles the user interface (what the user sees and
clicks).
2. Application Tier (Business Logic / Middle Tier)
- contains all business rules,
validation, and processing. This tier t
alks to the database on behalf of the client.
3. Data Tier (Database Server)
- stores and manages the actual data.
Working (Step by step):
1. Client sends a request (e.g., clicks "Submit Order") to the Application Server.
2. Application Server applies business rules (e.g., "check if stock is available").
3. Application Server builds and sends the SQL query to the Database Server.
4. Database Server executes the query and returns data to the Application Server.
5. Application Server processes/formats t
he result and sends it back to the Client.
Advantages: - Clients are "thin"
- they don't need heavy installation, just a browser
-
Business logic is centralized
- easy to update once, applies to everyone
- Better
security
- clients never touch the database directly
- Scales well
- multiple
application servers can be added (load balancing)
- Supports many concurrent users,
ideal for internet/web applications
Limitations:
- More complex to design, build, and debug
- More network
communication (extra hop) can
add slight delay
- Requires more hardware/servers, so
higher initial cost
Exam Tip: A very common exam question is "Differentiate between two
- tier and three
-
tier architecture." Always mention: number of layers, where business logic sits,
scalability, and typical use case.

title: Concurrency Control Techniques

overview.whatIsIt:
Concurrency control is the set of techniques a database uses to make sure
that when
many users/transactions access the database at the same time
, the data
stays correct and consistent.
overview.whyNeed:
If two people update the same bank account at the same time
without any control, money can be lost or duplicated. Concurrency control prevents
these errors.
Where is it u
sed? - Banking transaction systems
- Airline/train ticket booking systems
- Online shopping (stock/inventory updates)
- Any multi - user database application
overview.whereUsed: Enterprise banking, web applications, and large-scale data platforms.

Imagine two people trying to withdraw money from the
same joint bank account at the
same second, from two different ATMs. If the system does not control this carefully,
both withdrawals might succeed even if there isn't enough money for both
- because
each ATM checked the balance before the other one finished updating it
.

title: Introduction to Parallel Databases

overview.whatIsIt:
A parallel database system uses
multiple processors (CPUs) and multiple
disks working together
to perform database operations faster, by splitting one big task
into smaller pieces that run at the same time.
overview.whyNeed:
Modern applications handle huge amounts of data (big data, data
warehouses). A single processor cannot process billions of rows fast enough.
Parallelism speeds things up by dividing the work.
Wh ere is it used?
- Data warehousing and business intelligence
- Large - scale analytics
(Google, Facebook
- scale queries) - Scientific computing on massive datasets
overview.whereUsed: Enterprise banking, web applications, and large-scale data platforms.

beginnerIntro.story:
Imagine you must count all the votes in a national election. One person counting alone
would take days. Instead, you divide the ballot boxes among 100 people, each counts
their portion, and then someone adds up all the totals. This is exactly what a parallel
database does with data.

subsections.title: 4.1 Goals of Parallel Databases
subsections.content:
•
Speed - up: Doing the same amount of work faster by adding more processors.
•
Scale - up: Handling a proportionally larger job in the same amount of time by
adding proportionally more resources.

subsections.title: 4.2 Parallel Database Architectures
subsections.content:
There are three m
ain hardware architectures:
1.
Shared Memory Architecture
- All processors share the same main memory
and disk. Easy to program, but does not scale well beyond a limited number of
processors because memory becomes a bottleneck.
2.
Shared Disk Architecture
- Each processor has its own private memory but all
processors share the same disks. Offers good fault tolerance, but disk access can
become a bottleneck.
3.
Shared Nothing Architecture
- Each processor has its own private memory
AND its own private disk. Processor
s communicate only through a network. This
scales the best and is used by most modern large
- scale systems (e.g., Google
BigQuery, Teradata).

subsections.title: 4.3 Types of Parallelism
subsections.content:
1.
Interquery Parallelism
- Different queries (from different users) run in parallel
on different processors. Improves throughput for many simultaneous users.
2.
Intraquery Parallelism
- A single query is broken into parts that run in parallel.
This speeds up one individual (often large/complex) query.
-
Intraoperation Parallelism
- a single operation
(like a big sort or join) is
split across multiple processors, each working on a portion of the data.
-
Interoperation Parallelism
- different operations within the same query
run in parallel.
•
Pipeline Parallelism:
the output of one operation is fed directly
into the next operation while the first is still producing more
output (like an assembly line).
•
Independent Parallelism:
operations that do not depend on each
other's results run at the same time.

subsections.title: 4.4 Parallel Database Implementation Strategies
subsections.content:
•
Data Parti tioning: Splitting a large table's rows across multiple disks/nodes so
each node stores and processes only a portion.
-
Round - Robin Partitioning:
rows are distributed evenly, one by one, in
rotation across nodes
- good for balanced load, but not good for range
queries.
-
Hash Partitioning:
a hash function is applied to a chosen column to
decide which node stores the row
- good for equality lookups.
-
Range Partitioning:
rows are divided based on ranges of a key value (e.g.,
A-M on Node1, N
-Z on Node2)
- good for range queries, but can create
uneven load ("skew") if data is not uniform.
•
Parallel Query Optimization:
the query optimizer decides how to split
operations like joins and sorts across nodes for best performance.
•
Parallel Sort/Join Algorithms:
techniques li
ke parallel hash join and parallel
merge sort distribute the heavy computation across nodes.

title: Introduction to Distributed Databases

overview.whatIsIt: Core database architecture and management techniques.
overview.whyNeed: Crucial for scalability, data integrity, and high performance.
overview.whereUsed: Enterprise banking, web applications, and large-scale data platforms.

beginnerIntro.story:
Imagine a chain of supermarkets in different cities. Each store keeps its own local sales
records, but the head office can still ask, "How many total apples did we sell across all
stores today?" and get one combined answer. The data is physically spread out, but
logically it behaves like one big database.

subsections.title: 4.1 Distributed Databas
subsections.content:
e Architecture
•
Client - Server Distributed Architecture:
clients connect to different database
servers, and servers may need to communicate with each other to answer a
query spanning multiple sites.
•
Peer - to- Peer (Collaborating Server) Architecture:
every site runs full database
software and can act as both a client and a server; all sites cooperate as equals.
•
Homogeneous Distributed Database:
all sites use the same database
management system (DBMS) software and the same schema structure
- easier
to manage.
•
He terogeneous Distributed Database:
different sites may use different DBMS
software or schemas; requires extra translation layers (middleware) to
communicate
- more complex but more flexible for merging existing separate
systems.

subsections.title: 4.2 Key Concepts
subsections.content:
•
Fragmentation:
dividing a relation (table) into smaller pieces (fragments) and
storing them at different sites.
-
Horizontal Fragmentation:
splitting a table by
rows (e.g., customers from
North region at Site A, South region at Site B).
-
Vertical Fragmentation:
splittin g a table by columns (e.g., basic customer
info at Site A, financial info at Site B).
-
Mixed (Hybrid) Fragmentation:
a combination of horizontal and vertical

if one site goes down, other sites can

subsections.content:

Key - Value Store
- data is stored as simple key
- value pairs, like a giant
dictionary (e.g., Redis, DynamoDB). Extremely fast for simple lookups.

- like documents that can have
nested structures (e.g., MongoDB, CouchDB). Good for semi
- structured data.

Column - Family Store
- data is stored in columns grouped into families rather
than rows, optimized for fast reads/writes over huge datasets (e.g., Cassandra,
HBase).
4.
Graph Database
- data is stored as
nodes and edges representing entities and
their relationships, ideal for highly connected data (e.g., Neo4j). Good for social
networks, recommendation engines.

subsections.content:
•
Unlike relational modeling (normalize into many related tables), NoSQL
modeling often
denormalizes
data - related information is stored together in
one document/record to avoid the cost of joins.

Data modeling is driven by
how the application will query the data
, not by
minimizing redundancy (a very different philosophy from
SQL normalization).
•
Embedding related data (e.g., storing a customer's orders directly inside the
customer document) is common in document stores for fast reads.

subsections.content:

- \ $lt / \ $lte -
less than / less than or equal to
- \ $in - matches any value in a given list Example:

\ $gt: 80 } }) finds students with marks greater than 80.

at least one
of
multiple conditions.

\ $gt: 90 } } ] })

all conditions to be true (often i
mplicit
when listing multiple fields directly).

This is useful in flexible

subsections.title: 4.1 Introduction to the Aggregation Pipeline
subsections.content:
The aggregation pipeline
is MongoDB's primary and most powerful framework for data
processing. It consists of multiple
stages , each transforming the documents before
passing them to the next stage. Common stages include:
- \ $match
- filters
documents (similar to WHERE in SQL).
- \ $group - groups documents by a specified
fiel d and computes aggregate values (similar to GROUP BY).
- \ $sort - sorts
documents based on a field.
- \ $project - reshapes documents, selecting/computing
specific fields (similar to projection/SELECT).
- \ $limit /
\ $skip - restrict or skip a
number of documents (useful for pagination).
Example pipeline (average marks per department):
db.students.aggregate([
{ \ $match: { marks: {
\ $gte: 40 } } },
{ \ $group: { _id: "
\ $department", avgMarks: {
\ $avg: " \ $marks" } } },
{ \ $sort: { avgMarks:
- 1 } }
])
This filter s passing students, groups them by department, computes the average marks
per department, and sorts departments by highest average.

subsections.title: 4.2 Aggregation Using MapReduce
subsections.content:
•
MapReduce is an older, more general
- purpose technique for processing large
datasets using two custom JavaScript functions:
-
Map function
- processes each document and emits key
- value pairs.
-
Reduce function
- combines all values for each key into a single
summarized result.
•
MapReduce is more flexible for very complex, custom processing logic, but i
t is
generally slower and more complex to write than the aggregation pipeline.
•
Modern MongoDB usage strongly favors the aggregation pipeline over
MapReduce for most tasks, since the pipeline is faster and easier to understand.

subsections.title: 4.3 Single - Purpose Aggregation Operations
subsections.content:
MongoDB also provides simple, built
- in functions for basic, common aggregation tasks
without needing a full pipeline:
- count() - returns the number of documents matching
a query.
- distinct()
- returns the unique values for a specified field
across the
collection. These are convenient for quick, simple summaries when a full aggregation
pipeline is not necessary.

title: Basics of Transactions and ACID Properties

overview.whatIsIt:
A transaction
is a single logical unit of work in a database, made up of one
or more operations, that must be executed completely or not at all.
ACID is a set of
four properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) that guarantee
transactions are processed reliably.
overview.whyNeed:
Without these guarantees, a system crash or concurrent access
could leave data in a broken, inconsistent, or partially updated state
- a serious risk for
critical systems like banking.
overview.whereUsed:
- Banking and financial systems
- E- commerce order processing
-
Airline reservation systems
- Any system where correctness of multi
- step operations
matters

beginnerIntro.story:
Think of transferring money from Account A to Account B. This requires two steps:
subtract from A,
add to B. If the system crashes after subtracting but before adding,
money disappears! A transaction bundles both steps together so that either
both
happen, or neither happens.

keywords.meaning: A group of operations treated as one single unit
Successfully finishing and saving a transaction permanently
Undoing a transaction's changes because something went wrong
All- or- nothing execution
Once saved, data survives even a crash

analogies.title: Money Transfer
analogies.description:
Withdrawing cash from one envelope and putting it in
another envelope must happen together
- you would never want to take money out
and then simply lose it if you got interrupted halfway.

analogies.title: Online Shopping Checkout
analogies.description:
Placing an order involves reducing stock,
charging payment, and creating an order record. If payment fails, the stock reduction
must also be undone
- all steps succeed together, or none of them do.

subsections.title: 4.1 What is a Transaction?
subsections.content:
A transaction moves a database from one
consistent state
to another. It typically ends
with either:
- Commit - all changes are made permanent.
- Rollback (Abort)
- all
changes are undone, as if the transaction never happened.

subsections.title: 4.2 The ACID Properties
subsections.content:
1.
Atomicity - a transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit; either
all its
operations complete successfully, or
none of them do. If any step fails, the entire
transaction is rolled back.
2.
Consistency
- a transaction must take the databas
e from one valid state to
another valid state, preserving all defined rules (constraints, triggers)
- it should
never leave the database violating its own rules.
3.
Isolation - concurrently executing transactions should not interfere with each
other; the result should be as if transactions ran one after another (serially), even
though they may actually run concurrently for performance.
4.
Durability - once a transaction commits, its changes are permanent and will
survive even a system crash or power failure (usua
lly achieved by writing
changes to non
- volatile storage/logs).

subsections.title: 4.3 Transaction States
subsections.content:
A transaction moves through these states during its lifecycle:
- Active - the

title: Real - Time Transaction Systems

overview.whatIsIt:
A real - time transaction system
is a database system where transactions
must be completed within a
strict, predictable time limit (dead
line) , not just "as fast
as possible" - correctness includes both the right result AND meeting the deadline.
overview.whyNeed:
Some applications (like flight control, medical monitoring,
industrial automation) fail dangerously if results arrive too late, even if the result itself
is correct. Regular database systems don't guarantee timing, only eventual correctness.
overview.whereUsed:
- Air traffic control systems
- Patient monitoring in hospitals (ICU
systems) - Industrial process control (factories, power
plants) - Stock trading systems
needing rapid response

beginnerIntro.story:
Imagine a fire alarm system
- even a perfectly accurate alert is useless if it takes 10
minutes to sound after a fire starts. In a real
- time transaction system, being "correct
but late" can be just as bad as being wrong.

analogies.description:
A car's airbag system must react within milliseconds
of a crash. A "correct" decision to deploy the airbag one second too late is completely
useless - timing is as important as correctness.

analogies.title: Live Sports Broadcast
analogies.description:
A slightly delayed video feed by a few seconds
might be acceptable (soft real
- time), but a pacemaker regulating a heartbeat cannot
tolerate delay at all (hard real
- time) - the required strictness of timing varies by
application.

subsections.title: 4.1 Characteristics of Real
subsections.content:
- Time Transactions
•
Transactions have an associated
deadline - a time by which they must
complete.
•
Correctness is defined by
both the logical result AND meeting the timing
constraint.
•
Traditional concurrency control (like standard 2PL) may need modification,
since blocking/waiting for locks can cause d
eadlines to be missed.

subsections.title: 4.2 Types of Real
subsections.content:
- Time Systems
•
Hard Real
- Time Systems
- missing a deadline is considered a total system
failure (e.g., missile guidance, life
- support systems). Absolutely no exceptions
allowed.
•
Soft Real - Time Systems
- missing a deadline reduces the value/quality of the
result but does not cause total failure (e.g., video streaming, some financial
trading systems).
•
Firm Real - Time Systems
- a middle ground; late results are considered useless
(the value drops to zero) but do not cause
a catastrophic failure, unlike hard
real - time.

subsections.title: 4.3 Scheduling in Real
subsections.content:
- Time Transaction Systems
Since correctness depends on timing, transaction scheduling must consider
deadlines, not just fairness or throughput:
- Earliest Deadline First (EDF)
- prioritize the transaction with the closest/soonest
deadline.
- Priority - based scheduling
- assign priorities based on how critical or urgent a
transaction is.
- Concurrency control protocols may need to be
deadline - aware , sometimes allowing
a lower - priority transa
ction to be aborted/preempted if it risks blocking a higher
-
priority, more urgent transaction.

subsections.title: 4.4 Challenges
subsections.content:
•
Balancing strict timing requirements with the correctness guarantees (like ACID)
of traditional transactions is difficult.
•
Predicting exactly how long a transaction will take (worst
- case execution time)
is hard in complex systems.
•
Locking - based concurrency control can cause
priority inversion
(a high -
priority transaction waiting on a lock held by a low
- priority one), which must be
specifically handl
ed in real - time systems.

overview.whatIsIt:
A long - duration transaction
is a transaction that
runs for a very long time
(minutes, hours, or even days)
- much longer than the typical short banking
transaction
- often because it involves human decision
- making or many connected
steps. Because standard transaction techniques (like holding locks for the whole
duration) don't work well for such long transactions, special
implementation
techniques - nesting, compensation, and specialized concurrency control
- are used.
overview.whyNeed:
If a long transaction held locks on data for hours or days (like
stan dard 2PL would require), it would block other users for an unacceptably long time.
Special techniques are needed to keep the system usable while still preserving
correctness as much as possible.
overview.whereUsed:
- Collaborative document editing over long periods
- Complex
engineering design processes (CAD projects)
- Long - running business processes (loan
processing, insurance claims)
- Travel booking systems (reserving flights, hotels, and
cars together)

beginnerIntro.story:
Imagine booking a
flight, hotel, and rental car together as one "trip package." If the
hotel booking fails after the flight is already booked, you don't want to hold the flight
seat locked for hours while you sort things out
- you'd rather book the flight, and if
something later fails, simply
cancel (compensate) that booking instead. This is the core
idea behind handling long
- duration transactions.

Standard concurrency control (like Strict 2PL) holds locks until commit
- fine

hours/days (other users get blocked for far too long).
•
Rolling back a long transaction entirely (as in a normal ACID rollback) can be
extremely wasteful if most of the work was actually valid and just one small part

A nested transaction

y of smaller
sub -

•
The overall (top

but nesting provides more fine

committed some of its sub

ailure occurs, a normal rollback isn't possible (the data is already

•
A compensating transaction
is a separate transaction specifically designed to
logically "undo" or reverse the effect of an earlier committed transaction (e.g., a
"cancel booking" transaction reversing a "make booking" transaction).
•
This concept underlies the popular
Saga pattern
, widely used in modern
distributed and microservice
- based systems, where each step has a matching
compensating acti
on ready to run if a later step fails.

subsections.content:

from multiple sources, organized for analysis (rather than daily transaction
processing).
•
Data mining typically operates
on top of
a data warehouse

provides clean, organized, historical data, and data mining techniques are
applied to that data to discover patterns.
•

subsections.title: 4.2 Association Rules
subsections.content:
•
Association rule mining
discovers relationships between items that frequently
occur together in data, typically expressed as "If A, then B" (e.g., "If a customer
buys bread, they often also buy butter").
•
Common measures used:

Support - how frequently the itemset appears in the data.
-

curs).

market basket analysis

recommendations.

subsections.content:
•
Classification
assigns data records into one of several
predefined
categories/classes
based on their attributes, using a model trained on historical
labeled data.
•
Example: classifying loan applicants as "high risk" or "low risk" based on income,
credit history, etc.
•
Common classification techniques include decision trees, Naive Bayes, and
neural networks (studied in more depth in machine
learning courses).

subsections.title: 4.4 Clustering
subsections.content:
•
Clustering
groups similar data records together
without predefined categories
- the groups (clusters) themselves are discovered from the data.
•
Example: grouping customers into segments based on purchasing behavior,
without knowing the segments in advance.
•
Common clustering techniques include K
- Means clustering and hierarchical
clustering.

title: Introduction to Business Intelligence

overview.whatIsIt:
Business Intelligence (BI)
refers to the technologies, tools, and processes
used to collect, integrate, analyze, and present business data to support better
decision - making by managers and executives.
overview.whyNeed:
Raw data and even data mining results need to be presented in a
clear, usable way (dashboards, reports) so that business leaders can quickly understand
trends and make informed decisions.
Where i s it used? - Executive dashboards
- Sales and marketing performance tracking
- Financial forecasting
- Operational efficiency monitoring
overview.whereUsed: Enterprise banking, web applications, and large-scale data platforms.

beginnerIntro.story:
If data mining is like digging for gold, Business Intelligence is like taking that gold and
turning it into a beautifully displayed, easy
- to- understand report or dashboard that a
manager can glance at and immediately understand what's happening in the business.

subsections.content:
•
Data Integration
- combining data from multiple sources (sales, finance,
operations) into one unified view.
•
Reporting and Dashboards
- presenting data visually (charts, graphs, KPIs) for
quick understanding.
•
Ad- hoc Querying
- allowing users to ask custom questions of the data without
needing a developer each time.
•
Trend Analysis and Forecasting
- identifying patterns over time to predict
future performance.
•
Self - Service Analytics
- empowering non
- technical business users to explore
data themselves.

subsections.content:
A typical BI framework/architecture includes:
1. Data Sources
- operational databases, external data, files.
2.ETL (Extra
ct, Transform, Load)
-
extracting data from sources,
transforming/cleaning it, and loading it into a data warehouse.

- organized storage for analysis.

- reporting, dashboards, OLAP (Online Analytical
Processing) tools.
5. Presentation Layer
- dashboards, visualizations, and reports delivered to end users.

subsections.title: 4.3 Types and Approaches for Machine Learning (in the context of BI)
subsections.content:
Modern BI increasingly incorporates
machine learning (ML)
to automate insight
discovery. Broad types of machine learning approaches include:
- Supervised Learning
- the model learns from labeled historical data (input
- output
pairs) to predict outcomes for new data (e.g., predicting customer churn based on past
labeled examples).
- Unsupervised Learning
- the model finds patterns/structure in data without
predefined labels (e.g., customer segmentation via clustering).
- Reinforcement Learning
-
the model learns by receiving feedback
(rewards/penalties) from its actions over time, impro
ving through trial and error (e.g.,
optimizing pricing strategies dynamically). These ML approaches enhance BI by
enabling predictive and prescriptive analytics, not just descriptive reporting of what
already happened.

subsections.content:
•
Store and manage
multimedia data types

combinations of these (unlike traditional databases limited to text/numbers).
•
Require special indexing and retrieval techniques, since searching "find images

•
Content - Based Retrieval
allows searching based on actual visual/audio features
(color, shape, texture, pitch), rather than relying only on manually added text
tags/descriptions.
•
Challenges include very large file sizes, the need for
efficient compression, and
complex similarity
- based searching (rather than exact matching).

and need to continue working offline.
•
Use synchronization
mechanisms to update the central database once the
device reconnects, resolving any conflicts that occurred during offline use.
•
Often need to be lightweight
(efficient on limited device
storage/battery/processing power).
